models.purpose: Place superchargers to cover demand at minimum transport cost.
models.summary: Nodes are 892 superchargers, 3,048 chargers and 497 cities, 4,295 in all, geocoded from Tesla.com through the Google Geocode API. Distances use a sphere of radius 6,378 km and shortest paths by SPFA. The objective minimizes the sum of assigned demand times distance. Each node must be covered, a share alpha of its demand must come from nodes beyond minD, and no node may hold more than maxC chargers. The program is too large for the simplex method, so it is solved as a minimum-cost maximum-flow with the Google OR-Tools cost-flow solver. Parameters: minD = 170 miles, alpha = 0.25, maxC = 50,000. Result: 873,869 superchargers for an all-electric US, split 40.25 percent urban, 25.38 suburban, 34.36 rural. South Korea, scaled by vehicles per capita, needs 56,953.

models.purpose: Date the adoption of electric vehicles with a Bass diffusion curve.
models.summary: The hazard of adoption is f(t) / (1 - F(t)) = p + q F(t), with F(0) = 0. The closed form is F(t) = (1 - exp(-bt)) / (1 + a exp(-bt)), where a = q/p and b = p + q, and the adoption rate peaks at t* = (1/b) ln(a). Fit to South Korean sales since 2012. Adoption reaches 10 percent in 2026, 30 percent in 2028, 50 percent in 2029 and 99.9 percent in 2036, counted from 2018.

models.purpose: Choose whether to build chargers or cars first.
models.summary: Two ratios, piles to cars and cars to a standard, define a two-by-two game. The mixed equilibrium for the car side is Pe = (EX40 - EX20) / (EX10 - EX20 - EX30 + EX40). A regression on 2012-2017 US data puts the stable car ratio at 0.375 and the stable pile ratio at 0.275. The rule: below 0.275 build piles, above it build cars, and keep the two investments within 10 million of the price ratio.
